disease_info: Acute Stress Disorder (ASD) is a time-limited trauma- and stressor-related condition that develops within days of exposure to an event involving actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violation, either directly, as a witness, or through close association. It is characterized by a cluster of intrusion, negative mood, dissociation, avoidance, and arousal symptoms lasting from 3 days to 1 month after the traumatic event, with clear associated functional impairment. Clinically, patients often present with marked distress and sudden changes in behavior or functioning shortly after the trauma, sometimes with dissociative experiences or pronounced hyperarousal. ASD is distinguished from posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) primarily by its shorter duration and earlier onset; persistent symptoms beyond one month raise concern for progression to PTSD or other comorbid conditions such as depression or substance use disorders.

narrative.stressor: Mario had been helping coordinate a small cultural booth at a downtown Colorado Springs street fair when a car suddenly plowed through a barricade, striking several pedestrians just a few yards from where he was arranging decorations. He watched one of the senior-center volunteers he knew well get hit and thrown to the pavement, and spent the next several minutes trying to follow shouted instructions from first responders while the scene was chaotic, bloody, and confusing. In the days that followed, his normally busy routine of gardening, art classes, and senior-center activities fell apart as he found himself unable to relax at home or return to the plaza, and even routine errands along busy streets became overwhelming enough that he began canceling commitments. When church friends noticed he had stopped coming to Mass and to the hiking group and he admitted he was "jumping out of his skin" at every small noise and feeling unsafe leaving his apartment, his parish priest and a neighbor from the senior center urged him to see a mental health professional through the clinic that partners with the parish.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Ever since that car drove into the crowd, even little sounds make me feel like I’m back there and I jump out of my chair or drop things.”

narrative.stressor: A week before presentation, Samona was driving home from an evening jazz event when a pickup truck ran a red light and slammed into the driver’s side of the car directly in front of her, causing it to spin and flip onto its roof. She narrowly avoided being hit herself, called 911, and waited on the roadside while first responders extracted the other driver, who appeared unconscious and badly injured; she later learned through local news that he remained in critical condition. In the days after, she tried to return to her precise, deadline-driven underwriting work, but found herself staring at spreadsheets without being able to stay at her desk, taking ride-shares instead of driving, and leaving early because she was shaken by any mention of the accident from coworkers who had seen the story. When she began turning down mentoring sessions with her high-school students, skipped her running club because she was afraid to cross busy intersections, and her manager commented on her uncharacteristic mistakes and absences, she recognized that her reaction to the crash was not easing and scheduled an urgent appointment through her company’s employee assistance program.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Since I watched that car get crushed in front of me, I’ve gone out of my way to avoid driving or even being near busy intersections.”

narrative.stressor: While on his delivery route late one evening, Lorenzo pulled up to an apartment complex just as a shooting broke out in the parking lot, with people running past his van and several rapid gunshots fired only a short distance away. He instinctively ducked behind his vehicle and stayed there until police arrived, later giving a brief statement before being released to finish his shift, though he never actually completed the remaining deliveries. Over the next week, he struggled to keep working his usual routes through the Westside and nearby neighborhoods, calling in sick, asking coworkers to cover certain areas, and skipping basketball league games because he felt unable to be in crowded lots or city blocks that reminded him of the incident. When his supervisor warned him that his attendance and route coverage were putting his job at risk and his pastor noticed he had abruptly stopped singing with the choir, Lorenzo admitted that the memory of the shooting was "stuck" in his head and that he was on edge all the time, prompting him to accept a referral to a community mental health clinic offered through his church’s outreach program.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Ever since I was there during that shooting, the scene keeps replaying in my head all day and I can’t shut it off.”
